extracted_claims.text: Article 43 of the adopted AI Act establishes two main conformity assessment routes for high-risk AI systems: assessment based on internal control (Annex VI) and assessment of the quality management system and technical documentation with involvement of a notified body (Annex VII).

For high-risk AI systems listed in point 1 of Annex III (biometrics), the provider may choose between internal control or a conformity assessment involving a notified body, with the choice depending on whether harmonised standards or common specifications under Articles 40/41 have been applied.

For high-risk AI systems referred to in points 2 to 8 of Annex III, providers must follow the conformity assessment procedure based on internal control under Annex VI, which does not involve a notified body.

For high-risk AI systems covered by existing EU sectoral legislation listed in Section A of Annex I, providers must follow the conformity assessment procedures of that sectoral legislation, with notified bodies verifying compliance with the AI-specific requirements of the Act.

Classification as high-risk does not itself require third-party conformity assessment where the applicable sectoral legislation allows reliance on harmonised standards or common specifications instead.

For most high-risk AI systems, conformity with legal requirements can be demonstrated by providers themselves through an internal (self-)assessment procedure rather than mandatory third-party certification.

Article 46 allows a Member State market surveillance authority, by way of derogation from Article 43 and upon a duly justified request, to authorise placing on the market or putting into service of specific high-risk AI systems for a limited period, for exceptional reasons of public security, protection of life and health, environmental protection, or protection of key industrial/infrastructural assets.

Only conformity assessment bodies that have been designated in accordance with the AI Act may carry out conformity assessments, and only for the activities/types of AI systems for which they are designated, per a list of codes and categories setting the scope of designation.

Article 31 sets requirements for notified bodies, including independence rules preventing conformity assessment personnel from being involved in the design, development, marketing or use of high-risk AI systems they assess.

The European Commission maintains the NANDO (New Approach Notified and Designated Organisations) database listing notified bodies designated under various EU regulations, including, going forward, the AI Act.

As of March 2026, the designation process for AI Act-specific notified bodies is ongoing and very few bodies have been fully designated specifically for AI Act conformity assessment; existing notified bodies under other product legislation (e.g., MDR, Machinery Regulation) can assess AI components within their existing scope, but AI-specific designation remains limited and is considered a bottleneck.

A Council document (Digital Omnibus on AI, deadline 26 February 2026) proposes a single application and single assessment procedure to facilitate designation of notified bodies under both the AI Act and sector-specific legislation, including for bodies already designated under other Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I Section A.
The NANDO system lists 51 MDR-designated notified bodies and 19 IVDR-designated bodies (per a 2025 EU evaluation document), with 12 MDR and 6 IVDR designation applications pending.

A 2026 industry tracker states that as of 12 October 2026, NANDO shows 52 bodies designated under MDR and 19 under IVDR (53 total), noting that designations and scopes can change and NANDO should be treated as the live source.

The MDCG 2025-6 guidance clarifies that for high-risk medical device AI (MDAI) classified under Article 6(1) AI Act, the relevant conformity assessment procedure is determined by the MDR/IVDR, and where both AI Act Annex I and Annex III could apply, Annex I prevails for that MDAI.

Guidance notes there is no official EU-published template or questionnaire for carrying out a conformity assessment under the AI Act, even though the assessment itself is required for high-risk systems.
An earlier 25 November 2022 proposal text of Article 43 (pre-adoption) set out similar but not identical conformity assessment procedures compared to the finally adopted Article 43.

The exact status and legal effect of the Digital Omnibus proposal (as of the February 2026 Council document) — whether it has been adopted, and what the final single-application/single-assessment procedure for notified bodies will look like — is unresolved in the sources.

Sources do not specify a current timeline or target date for when AI Act-specific notified body capacity will be considered 'sufficient' (unlike the CRA's stated target of 11 December 2026 for notified body capacity), creating uncertainty about when third-party conformity assessment under Annex VII will be practically available at scale.

The precise scope (codes/categories) of AI system types for which any notified body has so far been designated, referenced in the Council document ST-7322-2026-INIT, is not detailed in the available excerpts.

It is unclear from the sources which specific notified bodies (by name) have been designated to date for AI Act conformity assessment purposes, since available sources reference NANDO as the authoritative live source but do not reproduce an AI Act-specific list.
report:
# Conformity Assessment Procedures for High-Risk AI Systems Under the EU AI Act

## Executive Summary
The EU AI Act establishes a dual-track conformity assessment system under Article 43, combining internal control procedures (Annex VI) with notified-body-involved assessment (Annex VII) depending on the category of high-risk AI system ([artificialintelligenceact.eu](https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/article/43), [euaiact.com](https://www.euaiact.com/blog/eu-ai-act-conformity-assessment)). However, formal designation of notified bodies specifically for AI Act purposes remains limited and is widely flagged as a bottleneck, with current EU policy discussions (via a 2026 Digital Omnibus proposal) aiming to streamline the designation process ([Council document WK-3257-2026-INIT](https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/WK-3257-2026-INIT/en/pdf), [eyreact.com](https://eyreact.com/notified-bodies-ai-act)).

## Key Findings

### Conformity Assessment Procedures
Article 43 of the adopted AI Act establishes two main routes for high-risk AI systems: internal control (Annex VI), and assessment of the quality management system and technical documentation involving a notified body (Annex VII) (medium confidence) ([artificialintelligenceact.eu](https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/article/43), [euaiact.com](https://www.euaiact.com/blog/eu-ai-act-conformity-assessment)). For systems listed in point 1 of Annex III (biometrics), providers may choose between internal control or notified-body assessment, with the choice depending on whether harmonised standards or common specifications under Articles 40/41 have been applied (medium confidence) ([artificialintelligenceact.eu](https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/article/43), [dpo-consulting.com](https://www.dpo-consulting.com/blog/ai-conformity-assessment)). For systems in points 2–8 of Annex III, providers must follow internal control under Annex VI without notified body involvement (medium confidence) ([artificialintelligenceact.eu](https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/article/43)). Systems covered by existing EU sectoral legislation (Annex I, Section A) must follow that legislation's assessment procedures, with notified bodies verifying AI-specific compliance (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk, Art. 43](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43)). Notably, high-risk classification does not automatically require third-party assessment where sectoral legislation permits reliance on harmonised standards (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk, Art. 43](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43)). One low-confidence source suggests that for most high-risk systems, self-assessment rather than third-party certification suffices (low confidence) ([EDPB training materials](https://www.edpb.europa.eu/system/files/2025-06/spe-training-on-ai-and-data-protection-legal_en.pdf)).

Article 46 permits market surveillance authorities to derogate from Article 43 and authorise temporary market placement of specific high-risk systems for exceptional public security, health, environmental, or infrastructural reasons (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk, Art. 46](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-46)).

### Notified Body Requirements and Designation
Article 31 sets independence and competence requirements for notified bodies, preventing assessment personnel from involvement in design, development, marketing, or use of the systems they assess (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk, Art. 31](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-31)). Only bodies formally designated under the AI Act may conduct assessments, and only within their designated scope of codes/categories (medium confidence) ([Council document ST-7322-2026-INIT](https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/ST-7322-2026-INIT/en/pdf)). The European Commission's NANDO database tracks designated notified bodies across EU regulations, now extending to the AI Act (high confidence) ([single-market-economy.ec.europa.eu](https://single-market-economy.ec.europa.eu/single-market/goods/building-blocks/notified-bodies_en), [137ai.com](https://137ai.com/eu-notified-bodies.html)).

As of comparable medical-device regulations, NANDO lists 51–52 MDR-designated bodies and 19 IVDR-designated bodies, according to 2025–2026 sources ([EUR-Lex evaluation](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML?uri=CELEX%3A52025SC1051), [eucertify.com](https://eucertify.com/find-notified-body)) — though no equivalent AI Act-specific count is available. A low-confidence source states that as of March 2026, very few bodies have been fully designated specifically for AI Act assessment, with existing MDR/Machinery Regulation bodies able to assess AI components only within their existing scope (low confidence) ([eyreact.com](https://eyreact.com/notified-bodies-ai-act)). A Council document on a "Digital Omnibus on AI" (deadline 26 February 2026) proposes a single application/single assessment procedure to streamline designation across the AI Act and sectoral legislation (medium confidence) ([Council document WK-3257-2026-INIT](https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/WK-3257-2026-INIT/en/pdf)).

### Sector-Specific Interplay
MDCG 2025-6 guidance clarifies that for high-risk medical device AI, the MDR/IVDR determines the applicable conformity assessment procedure, with Annex I of the AI Act prevailing over Annex III where both could apply (medium confidence) ([health.ec.europa.eu](https://health.ec.europa.eu/document/download/b78a17d7-e3cd-4943-851d-e02a2f22bbb4_en)).

## Contradictions & Uncertainties
MDR notified body counts differ slightly between sources (51 vs. 52), likely reflecting normal changes over time rather than a true conflict ([EUR-Lex](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML?uri=CELEX%3A52025SC1051), [eucertify.com](https://eucertify.com/find-notified-body)). An earlier 2022 proposal text of Article 43 differs from the final adopted version and should not be treated as current law ([artificial-intelligence-act.com proposal](https://www.artificial-intelligence-act.com/Artificial_Intelligence_Act_Article_43_(Proposal_25.11.2022).html), [artificialintelligenceact.eu](https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/article/43)). Several claims carry low confidence (below 0.4), including the claim that self-assessment dominates for most high-risk systems, the claim regarding the current scarcity of AI Act-designated bodies, the absence of an official EU assessment template, and the 2026 MDR/IVDR count — these should be treated cautiously.

## Knowledge Gaps
No source provides a definitive current count of notified bodies formally designated specifically under the AI Act (as distinct from MDR/IVDR/Machinery Regulation). The legal status and final form of the Digital Omnibus proposal remain unresolved. There is no stated target date for achieving sufficient AI Act notified body capacity, unlike comparable timelines under the Cyber Resilience Act. The specific scope (by code/category) of any AI Act designations to date is not detailed in available sources, nor are the names of specific designated bodies.
